scenes.name: matrix multiplication: every row meets every column
scenes.visual: A visual step-by-step matrix multiplication of two 2x2 matrices A and B. Row 1 of A slides across column 1 of B to produce c11 = 19. The animation proves that for n x n matrices, every number is reused n times, contrasting matrix-vector decode (used once) with matrix-matrix prefill (used n times).

beats.say: To multiply two matrices, every row of the first meets every column of the second.
beats.show: Two 2x2 matrices A and B appear at center. Row 1 of A [1, 2] highlights, and Column 1 of B [5, 7] highlights.

beats.say: Multiply the pairs, add the products, and you get one entry of the result: one times five plus two times seven equals nineteen.
beats.show: Equation traces: '1 × 5 + 2 × 7 = 5 + 14 = 19'. The value 19 drops into entry c11 of matrix C.

beats.say: For two matrices of size n, calculating the output takes n cubed operations from two n squared numbers. Every single number is reused n times.
beats.show: A scaling formula appears: 'n × n × n tile takes n³ multiply-adds: each number is reused n times'.

beats.say: When matrix B has only one column, each weight is used once: that is decode. When B has many columns of tokens, every weight is reused: that is prefill.
beats.show: Matrix B collapses to 1 column: '1 column = decode (used once)'. Matrix B widens to 2,048 columns: '2,048 columns = prefill (used 2,048 times)'. Takeaway: 'matrix multiplication brings data reuse; matrix-vector multiplication does not'.

scenes.name: scalar unit against matrix tile
scenes.visual: A visual contrast between a scalar CUDA core and a Hopper tensor core. The CUDA core takes two numbers and adds a third. The tensor core executes D = A x B + C on whole matrix tiles, completing 512 multiply-adds in a single tick.

beats.say: A scalar C U D A core multiplies two numbers and adds a third, producing one number per cycle.
beats.show: A CUDA core executes: 'a × b + c = d' on scalar inputs, producing 1 output per cycle.

beats.say: A tensor core multiplies two small matrices and adds a third, producing a whole tile of outputs at once.
beats.show: A tensor core executes: 'D = A × B + C' on 2D tiles, illuminating a 2D matrix of outputs simultaneously.

beats.say: Inside Hopper, a single tensor core finishes five hundred and twelve multiply-adds every single tick: over a thousand operations per cycle.
beats.show: A hardware animation reveals the dense inner systolic structure of one Hopper tensor core: '512 multiply-adds per tick = 1,024 ops/tick'.

beats.say: One single warp instruction executes a sixteen by eight by sixteen step: two thousand and forty-eight multiply-adds, keeping one core busy for four ticks.
beats.show: A warp instruction packet (16×8×16) streams into the core: '2,048 multiply-adds · 4 ticks of execution'. Takeaway: 'one tensor instruction unleashes thousands of arithmetic operations'.

scenes.name: tile scaling and arithmetic reuse
scenes.visual: A logarithmic chart showing how increasing tile size multiplies data reuse. A 2x2 tile reuses numbers twice (1 op/byte); a 16x16 tile reuses numbers 16 times (8 ops/byte); a 128x128 tile reuses numbers 128 times (64 ops/byte).

beats.say: Bigger tiles feed themselves: the larger the tile, the more times each fetched number is reused.
beats.show: Tiles of expanding sizes draw on: 2x2, 4x4, 16x16, and 128x128.

beats.say: A two-by-two tile reuses each number twice, delivering one operation per byte.
beats.show: Bar at 2x2: '2 uses · 1 operation per byte'.

beats.say: A sixteen-by-sixteen tile reuses each number sixteen times: eight operations per byte. A tile a hundred and twenty-eight wide reuses each number a hundred and twenty-eight times.
beats.show: Bars climb: '16×16 · 16 uses (8 ops/byte)' → '128×128 · 128 uses (64 ops/byte)'.

beats.say: That is why tensor cores operate on tiles, why kernels stage large tiles in scratchpad memory, and why prefill saturates the hardware while decode cannot.
beats.show: A diagram shows a 128-wide tile staged in shared memory feeding tensor cores. Takeaway: 'data reuse grows with tile width: large tiles turn memory-bound workloads into compute-bound ones'.

scenes.name: why one operation gets its own silicon
scenes.visual: A pie chart showing that transformers spend over 90% of their arithmetic on matrix multiplications. A bar comparison shows peak spec sheet performance (989.4 TFLOP/s) versus sustained performance in well-tuned kernels (50% to 80%).

beats.say: Why dedicate five hundred and twenty-eight specialized units to a single mathematical operation?
beats.show: An aerial diagram of the H100 die highlights all 528 tensor cores across the 132 multiprocessors.

beats.say: Because modern transformers spend well over ninety percent of their arithmetic on matrix multiplication.
beats.show: A breakdown pie chart shows: 'Matrix Multiplications · 92%' in amber, with additions, layer norms, and activations taking the remaining 8%.

beats.say: Peak performance assumes every single unit is fed with data every single cycle without a stall. Real code never reaches it.
beats.show: A performance bar shows 'Peak specification · 989.4 TFLOP/s'.

beats.say: A superbly tuned kernel reaches fifty to eighty percent of peak. Compare chips on their peak; compare software on how close to peak it gets.
beats.show: A realistic performance band highlights: 'Well-tuned kernel · 50% to 80% of peak'. Takeaway pill: 'peak is a hardware ceiling; software quality is measured by what fraction of peak it sustains'.

checks.claim: 2,048 multiply-adds / 512 multiply-adds per tick = 4 ticks of execution
Tile reuse formula: n^3 ops / (2 * n^2 * 2 bytes) = n / 4 ops per byte; for 128x128 tile at 2 bytes: 2 * 128^3 / (3 * 128^2 * 2) = 85.3, or nxnxn tile doing 2*n ops / 4 bytes = n/2 ops/byte
